title: Four estates duplicate the discipline of generating a doc safely, not the provider code
body:
# 0028: Four estates duplicate the discipline of generating a doc safely, not the provider code

## Tags

helpers, seam, generated-docs, cross-estate

## Summary

Four Fly-deployed estates each needed to generate the factual half of a database runbook from live probes. Routed by conflab/vc via lamplight/vc as an architecture question: a builtin would put a fly.io opinion inside devbin and break `lib/cmd/db:16`, while four project handlers means four drift copies of the thing the exercise existed to remove.

## Reproduction

Not a defect report. An architecture ruling requested with a working ~90-line reference implementation offered as the starting point.

## Root Cause

The framing. All three shapes originally proposed assumed the FLY CODE was the thing to share. It is not. The provider verbs are cheap to write and trivial to verify, because you can just run them; what cost a measured incident is the DISCIPLINE of writing a generated file down safely. Conflab withdrew their shapes on that observation.

## Impact

Without a shared answer, four estates each reinvent five refusals, and the reference implementation offered as the starting point satisfied only three of them -- its author said so rather than letting it look finished.

## Proposed Fix

devbin owns the discipline; every project keeps its own producer.

## Related

- D5 / `lib/cmd/db:16` -- provider encoding stays project-local, which this honours rather than bends
- D15 -- the layering rule that decides the home
- 0025 -- the same week's lesson that adding to an artefact is a parser change

## Resolutions

**CLOSED 2026-08-24 (vc).** `generated_doc_write` in `lib/helpers`, with `docs/authoring-commands.md` carrying the worked example and `tests/unit/gendoc.bats` proving each refusal fires.

**It is a HELPER, not a command, and that is the substantive part of the ruling.** The three shapes offered were builtin, handler-per-project, or a new opt-in module. A function needs none of them: no catalogue row, no `opt-in` cell, no `@builtin`, no config schema key. It therefore costs devbin no new mechanism, which also sidesteps a hazard raised while assessing shape (c) -- the catalogue can express `opt-in` x `@builtin`, that cell is empty, and an unused cell is an untested cell.

The five refusals, each with an incident behind it in a consumer estate: a failed producer or empty output leaves the target untouched; `--deny-env VAR` refuses when VAR's value appears in the block; `--expect-lines` / `--expect-contains` refuse insufficient output; content outside the markers is copied through untouched and both markers must appear exactly once; the file is assembled in a temp beside the target and renamed.

**Four corrections to the spec as received.**

Markers are REQUIRED rather than defaulted. Any default encodes a comment syntax, and a framework shipping an HTML comment has decided its consumers write HTML -- which is precisely what the "devbin must not learn the output is Markdown" constraint forbids.

The temp goes BESIDE the target, not in `TMPDIR`. Rename is atomic only within a filesystem. `sed_inplace` already learned this; the pattern is now shared deliberately rather than twice by coincidence.

An unset or empty `--deny-env` variable is itself a refusal. **This was driven red before the branch existed** and is the reason the guard is worth having: an unset variable makes the check compare against the empty string, which every block contains, so the naive version refuses AND reports a leak. There was none. A wrong recorded reason is worse than none -- it sends the reader hunting a credential leak in a file that is fine while the real fault goes unread.

The artefact check owns sufficiency alone. The spec's producer refusal also covered a "short" block, which smuggles in a magic threshold; a guard with a magic number fires wrong. The producer refusal now keeps only the hard signals.

**No fsync, and the docs say so.** Shell has no portable fsync, so this buys atomicity and not durability. Claiming the other one would be the wrong kind of confident.

**Two of my own tests could not fail, and both were caught by asking what else would make them green.** The glob-literalness test used a block containing no `a`, which neither a glob nor a literal matches, so it passed either way; the discriminating input is `axxb` against a secret of `a*b`. And the temp-cleanup test used a failing producer, which returns at line 573 while the temp is created at line 638 -- it never reached the code it claimed to cover. The replacement reaches the branch via an unwritable directory, and the two post-temp failure paths are documented as UNCOVERED rather than left looking covered, because a test that cannot fail is worse than an absent one.
